# Let a three-dimensional vortex change its shape

[Project velocity. Evolve its rotational tendency. Watch new modes appear.]{.lesson-deck}
:::

The two-dimensional [exact vortex](../vorticity/index.qmd) keeps its shape
while viscosity changes its amplitude. This three-dimensional initial
field has a genuinely nonlinear evolution on $[0,2\pi)^3$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
u&=\sin x\cos y\cos z,\\
v&=-\cos x\sin y\cos z,\\
w&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taylor and Green's study provides the historical background for this
vortex family [@taylor1937]. Here the retained driver uses a small smoke
case to teach OpenPFC's Fourier vector operations and their diagnostics.

## Put the initial field in ordinary lambdas

```{.cpp include="../tg3d/verify.hpp" snippet="initial_velocity" dedent=2}
```

The third field starts at zero. That is an initial condition, not a
constraint maintained throughout the evolution: the nonlinear step can
produce a nonzero third velocity component. The retained tests explicitly
check that it does.

After transforming all three components, the helper uses the installed
projector and state filter:

```{.cpp include="../tg3d/verify.hpp" snippet="projection" dedent=2}
```

For a nonzero wave vector, the Leray projection removes the longitudinal
component of a vector $\widehat{\mathbf f}$:

$$
\widehat{P\mathbf f}
=\widehat{\mathbf f}
-\mathbf k\,\frac{\mathbf k\cdot\widehat{\mathbf f}}{|\mathbf k|^2}.
$$

The zero mode is left unchanged. Consistent odd derivative symbols handle
Nyquist components; the state-level two-thirds filter also removes the
high-frequency part of the initial state and subsequent stages.

## Use the installed rotational tendency

With $\boldsymbol\omega=\nabla\times\mathbf u$, the incompressible
velocity equation can be written

$$
\mathbf u_t=P(\mathbf u\times\boldsymbol\omega)
             +\nu\nabla^2\mathbf u.
$$

Projection removes the pressure-gradient contribution. The example
composes the public `ifrk4_velocity` and `rotational_tendency` operations,
with viscosity integrated through precomputed exponentials:

```{.cpp include="../tg3d/verify.hpp" snippet="velocity_step"}
```

The helper retains the existing one-rank ownership requirement. This
chapter does not change its solver or introduce a second velocity
projector alongside the installed library implementation.

## Define the norms before comparing them

At time zero, trigonometric orthogonality gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
E_0&=\tfrac12\langle u^2+v^2+w^2\rangle=\tfrac18,\\
\Omega_0&=\langle|\boldsymbol\omega|^2\rangle=\tfrac34.
\end{aligned}
$$

This driver's `enstrophy` column is the **full** mean squared vorticity.
The two-dimensional vorticity lesson's $Z$ contains an additional factor
of one half. Definitions, rather than column names alone, determine how
to compare those numbers.

The continuous periodic energy identity is

$$
\frac{dE}{dt}=-\nu\Omega.
$$

All initial modes have $|\mathbf k|^2=3$. Pure viscosity acting on that
initial shell would give

$$
E_{\mathrm{linear}}(t)=\tfrac18e^{-6\nu t}.
$$

The nonlinear tendency transfers energy between shells. Consequently the
`ke_linear` column is an initial-shell comparison, not an exact later-time
Navier–Stokes solution. A difference from that curve is not, by itself,
a numerical error.

## Run the bounded smoke case

From the repository root, with a compatible installed spectral CPU SDK:

```sh
mkdir -p results
openpfc compile examples/flow/taylor-green-3d/model.cpp --source-root examples/flow -o results/taylor-green
results/taylor-green --case smoke --outdir results/flow/taylor-green
```

Use one MPI rank, as required by this driver. The retained smoke case uses
$N=16$, $\nu=0.05$, $h=1/64$ and two steps, reaching $T=1/32$.
The [model](model.cpp) shares [verify.hpp](../tg3d/verify.hpp); keep their
relative layout when using downloaded sources. The CMake target remains
`taylor_green3d`, with its original build location and numerical tests.

Read `errors.csv`, `spectrum.csv` and `run.json`. The smoke case computes
diagnostics without a separately refined trajectory, so its solution-error
columns are empty. Treat those as unavailable comparisons, rather than
zero errors. Inspect divergence, energy, the third velocity component and
the shell-energy sum instead. At time zero, energy belongs to the
$|\mathbf k|^2=3$ shell; later rows can show transfer to other shells.

The existing tests verify the analytic initial norms, small divergence,
energy loss with positive viscosity, growth of the third component,
shell-energy normalization and common-grid restriction. Their criteria
remain unchanged. The retained larger `spatial` and `temporal` options
keep their existing fixed protocols; the smoke command is the small
entry point for this lesson.

In your own copy, change the initial amplitude and derive its time-zero
energy scaling before running. Then inspect which diagnostics test the
initial condition, which test incompressibility and which require a
separate grid or time reference. Keeping those questions distinct makes
a complex three-dimensional example teachable.
